claim: Action selection in the face of dynamic reward associations requires registering a change in value of the primary reinforcer.
source: Action selection in the face of dynamic reward associations requires several cognitive processes: registering a change in value of the primary reinforcer, adjusting the value of secondary reinforcers to reflect the new value of the primary reinforcer, and guiding action selection to optimal choices.
evidence: This is stated as part of the cognitive framework for understanding reinforcer devaluation tasks, drawing on established scientific understanding of the task components.

claim: Action selection in the face of dynamic reward associations requires adjusting the value of secondary reinforcers to reflect the new value of the primary reinforcer.
source: Action selection in the face of dynamic reward associations requires several cognitive processes: registering a change in value of the primary reinforcer, adjusting the value of secondary reinforcers to reflect the new value of the primary reinforcer, and guiding action selection to optimal choices.
evidence: This is stated as part of the cognitive framework for understanding reinforcer devaluation tasks, drawing on established scientific understanding of the task components.

claim: Action selection in the face of dynamic reward associations requires guiding action selection to optimal choices.
source: Action selection in the face of dynamic reward associations requires several cognitive processes: registering a change in value of the primary reinforcer, adjusting the value of secondary reinforcers to reflect the new value of the primary reinforcer, and guiding action selection to optimal choices.
evidence: This is stated as part of the cognitive framework for understanding reinforcer devaluation tasks, drawing on established scientific understanding of the task components.

claim: Flexible responding has been evaluated extensively using reinforcer devaluation tasks.
source: Flexible responding has been evaluated extensively using reinforcer devaluation tasks.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Performance on reinforcer devaluation tasks relies upon amygdala.
source: Performance on this task relies upon amygdala, Areas 11 and 13 of orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), and mediodorsal thalamus (MD).
evidence: This is supported by references to prior literature establishing the neural circuit underlying reinforcer devaluation.

claim: Performance on reinforcer devaluation tasks relies upon Areas 11 and 13 of orbitofrontal cortex (OFC).
source: Performance on this task relies upon amygdala, Areas 11 and 13 of orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), and mediodorsal thalamus (MD).
evidence: This is supported by references to prior literature establishing the neural circuit underlying reinforcer devaluation.

claim: Performance on reinforcer devaluation tasks relies upon mediodorsal thalamus (MD).
source: Performance on this task relies upon amygdala, Areas 11 and 13 of orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), and mediodorsal thalamus (MD).
evidence: This is supported by references to prior literature establishing the neural circuit underlying reinforcer devaluation.

claim: Differential contributions of amygdala and Areas 11 and 13 of OFC to specific sub-processes of reinforcer devaluation have been established.
source: Differential contributions of amygdala and Areas 11 and 13 of OFC to specific sub-processes have been established, but the role of MD in these sub-processes is unknown.
evidence: This statement references prior research that has characterized the roles of these brain regions.

claim: The role of MD in sub-processes of reinforcer devaluation is unknown.
source: Differential contributions of amygdala and Areas 11 and 13 of OFC to specific sub-processes have been established, but the role of MD in these sub-processes is unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of the macaque MD during specific phases of reinforcer devaluation revealed that MD is required for reward valuation.
source: Pharmacological inactivation of the macaque MD during specific phases of this task revealed that MD is required for reward valuation and action selection.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of the macaque MD during specific phases of reinforcer devaluation revealed that MD is required for action selection.
source: Pharmacological inactivation of the macaque MD during specific phases of this task revealed that MD is required for reward valuation and action selection.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: The profile of MD function in reinforcer devaluation is unique, differing from both amygdala and subregions of the OFC.
source: This profile is unique, differing from both amygdala and subregions of the OFC.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the current findings to prior literature on amygdala and OFC function.

claim: In daily life, reward contingencies are often unstable.
source: In daily life, reward contingencies are often unstable; an action that once produced a valued outcome may over time become less desirable.
evidence: This is a general statement about behavior based on common knowledge.

claim: The ability to shift responses away from previously valued action-outcome pairs is a hallmark example of behavioral flexibility.
source: The ability to shift responses away from the previously valued action-outcome pair is a hallmark example of behavioral flexibility.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about behavioral flexibility based on established scientific understanding.

claim: Flexible responding has been evaluated extensively through the use of reinforcer devaluation tasks.
source: Flexible responding (i.e., adapting behavior to reflect new reward contingencies or reward values) has been evaluated extensively through the use of reinforcer devaluation tasks (Málková et al., 1997; Hatfield et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In reinforcer devaluation tasks, the value of secondary reinforcers or operanda decrease following an experimental reduction in the value of the associated primary reinforcer.
source: In these tasks, the value of secondary reinforcers or operanda (e.g., objects), and actions that were once favored decrease following an experimental reduction in the value of the associated primary reinforcer.
evidence: This describes the basic mechanism of the reinforcer devaluation task based on established methodology.

claim: Optimal performance in the reinforcer devaluation task requires registering a change in value of the primary reinforcer.
source: Processes required for optimal performance in the reinforcer devaluation task include: [1] registering a change in value of the primary reinforcer, [2] integrating the new value of the primary reinforcer with the cognitive representation of the secondary reinforcers/operanda (e.g., objects that signal the reward), and [3] guiding action selection to target the now optimal choice.
evidence: This is stated as part of the cognitive framework for understanding the task.

claim: Optimal performance in the reinforcer devaluation task requires integrating the new value of the primary reinforcer with the cognitive representation of the secondary reinforcers/operanda.
source: Processes required for optimal performance in the reinforcer devaluation task include: [1] registering a change in value of the primary reinforcer, [2] integrating the new value of the primary reinforcer with the cognitive representation of the secondary reinforcers/operanda (e.g., objects that signal the reward), and [3] guiding action selection to target the now optimal choice.
evidence: This is stated as part of the cognitive framework for understanding the task.

claim: Optimal performance in the reinforcer devaluation task requires guiding action selection to target the now optimal choice.
source: Processes required for optimal performance in the reinforcer devaluation task include: [1] registering a change in value of the primary reinforcer, [2] integrating the new value of the primary reinforcer with the cognitive representation of the secondary reinforcers/operanda (e.g., objects that signal the reward), and [3] guiding action selection to target the now optimal choice.
evidence: This is stated as part of the cognitive framework for understanding the task.

claim: In the standard version of the reinforcer devaluation task used in macaques, animals are trained to associate sets of objects with one of two rewards.
source: In the standard version of this task used in macaques, animals are trained to associate sets of objects with one of two rewards (primary reinforcers; e.g., peanuts or fruit snacks).
evidence: This describes the standard methodology of the task.

claim: After the association between objects and particular rewards is established, subjects are presented with a forced choice between objects associated with each of the two foods.
source: After the association between objects and particular rewards is established, subjects are presented with a forced choice between objects associated with each of the two foods.
evidence: This describes the standard methodology of the task.

claim: The proportion of choices between objects rewarded with one type of food versus the other represents the baseline preference.
source: The proportion of choices between the objects rewarded with one type of food (e.g., peanuts) versus the other (e.g., fruit snacks) represents the baseline preference.
evidence: This defines a key measure used in the task.

claim: An experimental reduction of reward value by selective satiation produces a devaluation effect.
source: An experimental reduction of reward value by selective satiation (i.e., providing one food to satiety) produces a devaluation effect, i.e., a decrease in the proportion of objects associated with the sated food that are selected.
evidence: This describes the expected outcome of the devaluation procedure.

claim: The devaluation effect is a decrease in the proportion of objects associated with the sated food that are selected.
source: An experimental reduction of reward value by selective satiation (i.e., providing one food to satiety) produces a devaluation effect, i.e., a decrease in the proportion of objects associated with the sated food that are selected.
evidence: This defines what constitutes a devaluation effect.

claim: Reinforcer devaluation processes critically rely on an interactive network including the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), the amygdala, and the mediodorsal thalamus (MD).
source: These processes critically rely on an interactive network including the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), the amygdala, and the mediodorsal thalamus (MD).
evidence: This statement is supported by references to prior literature establishing the neural circuit.

claim: The amygdala projects directly to OFC.
source: The amygdala projects directly to OFC, and indirectly to the OFC via the MD (Timbie and Barbas, 2015).
evidence: This anatomical fact is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The amygdala projects indirectly to the OFC via the MD.
source: The amygdala projects directly to OFC, and indirectly to the OFC via the MD (Timbie and Barbas, 2015).
evidence: This anatomical fact is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MD is reciprocally interconnected with Areas 11 and 13 of the OFC.
source: MD is reciprocally interconnected with two critical subregions of the OFC, Areas 11 and 13 (Ray and Price, 1993).
evidence: This anatomical fact is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Lesions to the amygdala impair the typical shift away from objects that predict the sated food.
source: Lesions to each of these nodes impair the typical shift away from the objects that predict the sated food (Málková et al., 1997; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Izquierdo and Murray, 2010; Browning et al., 2015; Pickens, 2008; Mitchell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior lesion studies.

claim: Lesions to Areas 11 and 13 of OFC impair the typical shift away from objects that predict the sated food.
source: Lesions to each of these nodes impair the typical shift away from the objects that predict the sated food (Málková et al., 1997; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Izquierdo and Murray, 2010; Browning et al., 2015; Pickens, 2008; Mitchell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior lesion studies.

claim: Lesions to MD impair the typical shift away from objects that predict the sated food.
source: Lesions to each of these nodes impair the typical shift away from the objects that predict the sated food (Málková et al., 1997; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Izquierdo and Murray, 2010; Browning et al., 2015; Pickens, 2008; Mitchell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior lesion studies.

claim: Crossed lesions of any two nodes of the amygdala-OFC-MD circuit impair performance on reinforcer devaluation.
source: Moreover, crossed lesions of any two nodes of this circuit likewise impair performance.
evidence: This statement is supported by the context of prior lesion studies.

claim: Lesions do not have the temporal specificity needed to dissociate the contributions of brain regions during discrete phases of task performance.
source: While lesions provide strong evidence that these brain regions are required for task performance, they do not have the temporal specificity needed to dissociate the contributions during discrete phases of task performance.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration based on the nature of lesion studies.

claim: Focal pharmacological manipulations can transiently suppress activity within a brain region.
source: By contrast, focal pharmacological manipulations, which can transiently suppress activity within a brain region, have revealed differential roles for the amygdala and the OFC in particular phases of this task (Wellman et al., 2005; West et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the methodological advantage of pharmacological inactivation, supported by citations.

claim: Focal pharmacological manipulations have revealed differential roles for the amygdala and the OFC in particular phases of reinforcer devaluation.
source: By contrast, focal pharmacological manipulations, which can transiently suppress activity within a brain region, have revealed differential roles for the amygdala and the OFC in particular phases of this task (Wellman et al., 2005; West et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior pharmacological inactivation studies.

claim: Neither the amygdala nor the OFC are needed to register a change in value of the primary reinforcer.
source: While neither the amygdala, nor the OFC are needed to register a change in value of the primary reinforcer, both structures play critical and differential roles in the subsequent processes.
evidence: This is based on prior pharmacological inactivation studies.

claim: The amygdala is necessary for adjusting the object representations to reflect the new value of the primary reinforcer.
source: The amygdala is necessary for adjusting the object representations to reflect the new value of the primary reinforcer, but not necessary for optimal action selection (Wellman et al., 2005); a similar profile has also been observed for the OFC Area 13.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The amygdala is not necessary for optimal action selection in reinforcer devaluation.
source: The amygdala is necessary for adjusting the object representations to reflect the new value of the primary reinforcer, but not necessary for optimal action selection (Wellman et al., 2005); a similar profile has also been observed for the OFC Area 13.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: OFC Area 13 is necessary for adjusting the object representations to reflect the new value of the primary reinforcer.
source: The amygdala is necessary for adjusting the object representations to reflect the new value of the primary reinforcer, but not necessary for optimal action selection (Wellman et al., 2005); a similar profile has also been observed for the OFC Area 13.
evidence: This is stated based on prior findings.

claim: OFC Area 13 is not necessary for optimal action selection in reinforcer devaluation.
source: The amygdala is necessary for adjusting the object representations to reflect the new value of the primary reinforcer, but not necessary for optimal action selection (Wellman et al., 2005); a similar profile has also been observed for the OFC Area 13.
evidence: This is implied by the statement that Area 13 has a similar profile to the amygdala.

claim: OFC Area 11 is critical only for action selection in reinforcer devaluation.
source: By contrast, Area 11 is critical only for action selection (Murray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MD receives input from amygdala.
source: Because MD receives input from amygdala and is reciprocally connected with both Areas 11 and 13 of the OFC (Timbie and Barbas, 2015), it suggests that this structure may be central to the devaluation circuit.
evidence: This anatomical fact is supported by citation.

claim: MD is reciprocally connected with both Areas 11 and 13 of the OFC.
source: Because MD receives input from amygdala and is reciprocally connected with both Areas 11 and 13 of the OFC (Timbie and Barbas, 2015), it suggests that this structure may be central to the devaluation circuit.
evidence: This anatomical fact is supported by citation.

claim: The anatomical connectivity of MD suggests that this structure may be central to the devaluation circuit.
source: Because MD receives input from amygdala and is reciprocally connected with both Areas 11 and 13 of the OFC (Timbie and Barbas, 2015), it suggests that this structure may be central to the devaluation circuit.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical connectivity.

claim: The role of the MD in specific phases of devaluation is unknown.
source: However, the role of the MD in specific phases of devaluation is unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Four adult male rhesus macaques were tested on a reinforcer devaluation task while transiently inactivating the MD during various stages of the task.
source: To dissociate between these outcomes, we tested four adult male rhesus macaques on a reinforcer devaluation task while transiently inactivating the MD during various stages of the task (Málková et al., 1997).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach of the study.

claim: Animals were trained on a set of forty concurrent object discriminations.
source: Animals were first trained on a set of forty concurrent object discriminations; through repeated trials the animals learned the association between each object and a particular reward (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the training procedure used in the study.

claim: Through repeated trials, animals learned the association between each object and a particular reward.
source: Animals were first trained on a set of forty concurrent object discriminations; through repeated trials the animals learned the association between each object and a particular reward (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the outcome of the training procedure.

claim: Animals were tested for preference on a baseline object probe test.
source: Next, they were tested for preference on a baseline object probe test (baseline probe).
evidence: This describes the testing procedure used in the study.

claim: In the baseline probe test, two objects, each baited with one of the two foods, were pitted against each other.
source: In this test, two objects, each baited with one of the two foods, were pitted against each other.
evidence: This describes the procedure of the baseline probe test.

claim: Animals underwent selective satiation and were tested on an object probe test (sated probe).
source: On another day, animals underwent selective satiation (pre-feeding with one of the two foods) and were again tested on an object probe test (sated probe), administered in a similar way as the baseline probe.
evidence: This describes the testing procedure used in the study.

claim: The weekly sequence of baseline probe followed by sated probe was repeated such that each food was sated for each experimental condition.
source: This weekly sequence (baseline probe followed by sated probe) was repeated such that each food was sated for each experimental condition (see Figure 1 for experimental timeline).
evidence: This describes the experimental design, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: In the probe tests, the animal selected between two objects, each baited with one of the two food rewards.
source: In the above probe tests, the animal selected between two objects, each baited with one of the two food rewards.
evidence: This describes the procedure of the probe tests.

claim: The objects were the cue used to guide action in the probe tests.
source: Thus, the objects were the cue used to guide action.
evidence: This describes the role of objects in the task.

claim: Animals were tested in a 'consummatory' probe, in which they chose between two competing food rewards in the absence of objects.
source: We also tested animals in a 'consummatory' probe, in which they chose between two competing food rewards in the absence of objects; this served as a control to ensure successful devaluation of the primary reinforcer.
evidence: This describes a control test used in the study.

claim: The consummatory probe served as a control to ensure successful devaluation of the primary reinforcer.
source: We also tested animals in a 'consummatory' probe, in which they chose between two competing food rewards in the absence of objects; this served as a control to ensure successful devaluation of the primary reinforcer.
evidence: This describes the purpose of the consummatory probe.

claim: A shift in choices between the baseline and sated probe tests is reflected by a positive proportion shifted.
source: A shift in choices between the baseline and sated probe tests is reflected by a positive proportion shifted (see Materials and methods) and indicates successful devaluation.
evidence: This defines the measure used to assess devaluation.

claim: A positive proportion shifted indicates successful devaluation.
source: A shift in choices between the baseline and sated probe tests is reflected by a positive proportion shifted (see Materials and methods) and indicates successful devaluation.
evidence: This defines what a positive proportion shifted means.

claim: A proportion shifted value of 1 indicates a complete shift away from objects predicting the sated food.
source: A value of 1 indicates a complete shift away from objects predicting the sated food, a value of 0 indicates no shift in preference.
evidence: This defines the interpretation of the proportion shifted measure.

claim: A proportion shifted value of 0 indicates no shift in preference.
source: A value of 1 indicates a complete shift away from objects predicting the sated food, a value of 0 indicates no shift in preference.
evidence: This defines the interpretation of the proportion shifted measure.

claim: Decreases in proportion shifted after experimental manipulations indicate impaired reinforcer devaluation.
source: Thus, decreases in proportion shifted after experimental manipulations indicate impaired reinforcer devaluation.
evidence: This defines how impairments are assessed in the study.

claim: Muscimol (9 nmol) was microinjected into the MD on separate testing weeks.
source: On separate testing weeks, we microinjected the GABAa receptor agonist muscimol (MUS, 9 nmol), the glutamate receptor antagonist kynurenic acid (KYNA, 450 nmol), or saline into the MD, either prior to selective satiation or prior to the sated probe test (Figures 2A1–4).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation used in the study.

claim: Kynurenic acid (450 nmol) was microinjected into the MD on separate testing weeks.
source: On separate testing weeks, we microinjected the GABAa receptor agonist muscimol (MUS, 9 nmol), the glutamate receptor antagonist kynurenic acid (KYNA, 450 nmol), or saline into the MD, either prior to selective satiation or prior to the sated probe test (Figures 2A1–4).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation used in the study.

claim: Saline was microinjected into the MD on separate testing weeks.
source: On separate testing weeks, we microinjected the GABAa receptor agonist muscimol (MUS, 9 nmol), the glutamate receptor antagonist kynurenic acid (KYNA, 450 nmol), or saline into the MD, either prior to selective satiation or prior to the sated probe test (Figures 2A1–4).
evidence: This describes the control condition used in the study.

claim: Drugs were microinjected either prior to selective satiation or prior to the sated probe test.
source: On separate testing weeks, we microinjected the GABAa receptor agonist muscimol (MUS, 9 nmol), the glutamate receptor antagonist kynurenic acid (KYNA, 450 nmol), or saline into the MD, either prior to selective satiation or prior to the sated probe test (Figures 2A1–4).
evidence: This describes the timing of drug infusions in the study.

claim: MRI-guided stereotaxic targeting of the MD was performed and confirmed.
source: MRI-guided stereotaxic targeting of the MD was performed and confirmed (Figure 2B) as we have described for other regions (Wellman et al., 2005; West et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the targeting method used in the study, with reference to Figure 2B and citations to prior work.

claim: Drug or vehicle was microinjected at one of two time points during the task to dissociate potential impairments in value updating from impairments in action selection.
source: We microinjected drug or vehicle at one of these two points during the task (see Figure 2A), to dissociate potential impairments in value updating (infusion before satiation; Figure 2A1 and A3) from impairments in action selection (infusion prior to probe; 2A2, 2A4).
evidence: This describes the experimental design rationale.

claim: Under baseline conditions, animals displayed a slight, but significant, preference for one type of reward.
source: Under baseline conditions, animals displayed a slight, but significant, preference for one type of reward (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The baseline preference pattern is similar to what has been previously reported.
source: This pattern is similar to what has been previously reported (Mitchell et al., 2007; West et al., 2011).
evidence: This compares the current finding to prior literature.

claim: Under saline-infused condition, animals displayed robust devaluation following satiation.
source: Under saline-infused condition, animals displayed robust devaluation following satiation; the devaluation effect was demonstrated by a shift away from choices of objects associated with the devalued food.
evidence: This is a finding from the control condition of the study.

claim: Microinjection of MUS either before satiation or before the sated probe test significantly disrupted the devaluation effect compared to sham/saline infusion.
source: Microinjection of MUS either before satiation or before the sated probe test significantly disrupted the devaluation effect compared to sham/saline infusion; this was manifest as a decrease in the proportion shifted (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The disruption of devaluation by MUS was evident in all four subjects.
source: This disruption was evident in all four subjects, resulting in a significant main effect of treatment (F1.1,3.4=13.3; p=0.029).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: MUS infusion before satiation significantly impaired performance compared to control.
source: Pairwise comparisons revealed a significant impairment in performance when MUS was infused either before satiation (p=0.032) or before the sated probe test (p=0.035).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: MUS infusion before the sated probe test significantly impaired performance compared to control.
source: Pairwise comparisons revealed a significant impairment in performance when MUS was infused either before satiation (p=0.032) or before the sated probe test (p=0.035).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: The magnitude of impairment did not differ between MUS infusion before satiation and before the probe test.
source: The magnitude of impairment did not differ between these conditions (p=0.13).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: MUS injection failed to alter choices in the consummatory probe.
source: In contrast to the object probe sessions, MUS injection failed to alter choices in the consummatory probe (Figure 2D; F1.3,4.0=1.25; p=0.35).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Animals still displayed a typical shift away from sated primary reinforcers in the consummatory probe after MUS injection.
source: Because animals still displayed a typical shift away from sated primary reinforcers in the consummatory probe, the deficits seen in Figure 2C cannot be explained by impairment in satiety or valuation of primary reinforcers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in the consummatory probe.

claim: The deficits in devaluation after MUS injection cannot be explained by impairment in satiety or valuation of primary reinforcers.
source: Because animals still displayed a typical shift away from sated primary reinforcers in the consummatory probe, the deficits seen in Figure 2C cannot be explained by impairment in satiety or valuation of primary reinforcers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in the consummatory probe.

claim: The disruption in the devaluation effect after MUS injection was specific to adjusting the value of the objects to reflect the new value of the primary reinforcer.
source: Thus, the disruption in the devaluation effect was specific to adjusting the value of the objects to reflect the new value of the primary reinforcer (i.e., the sated food).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of results.

claim: MUS injection was associated with a small, but significant impairment in concurrent visual discrimination.
source: To determine if deficits in devaluation were secondary to impaired object recognition, we tested animals (on a separate test day) on the concurrent visual discrimination task following drug infusion. MUS injection was associated with a small, but significant impairment in concurrent visual discrimination (Figure 2E; t = 4.09, df = 3, p=0.026).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The impairment in concurrent visual discrimination after MUS injection is possibly due to a drug-related deficit in object recognition, reward associations, and/or appropriate action selection.
source: It is possible that this finding is due to a drug-related deficit in object recognition, reward associations, and/or appropriate action selection.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of the observed deficit.

claim: The deficit in concurrent visual discrimination likely contributed to the significant decrease in baseline preference ratio observed after MUS injection.
source: Interestingly, this deficit also likely contributed to the significant decrease in baseline preference ratio (see Materials and methods) observed after MUS injection (Figure 2F; t = 4.28, df = 3, p=0.023).
evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between two observed effects.

claim: MUS presence abolished the baseline preference ratio.
source: Indeed, unlike under baseline (non-sated) condition when animals typically choose significantly more objects associated with one type of reward over the other, MUS presence abolished this baseline preference ratio (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: MUS injection produces long lasting inhibition, with effects evident for hours after drug injection.
source: MUS injection produces long lasting inhibition, with effects evident for hours after drug injection (Dybdal et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Injection of MUS before satiation likely results in a suppression of the activity within MD both during satiation and the probe test.
source: Thus, injection before satiation likely results in a suppression of the activity within MD both during satiation and the probe test.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known duration of action of MUS.

claim: Injections of MUS both before and after satiation disrupted devaluation.
source: Because injections both before and after satiation disrupted devaluation, these data alone were unable to clarify what, if any, role the MD played during the period of selective satiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MUS data.

claim: KYNA has a short duration of action (~30 min).
source: To determine if the MD is required specifically during selective satiation, we next turned to microinjection of KYNA, which has a short duration of action (~30 min) (Forcelli et al., 2014) and short half-life within the brain (8–30 min) (Vécsei and Beal, 1990; Turski and Schwarcz, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KYNA has a short half-life within the brain (8–30 min).
source: To determine if the MD is required specifically during selective satiation, we next turned to microinjection of KYNA, which has a short duration of action (~30 min) (Forcelli et al., 2014) and short half-life within the brain (8–30 min) (Vécsei and Beal, 1990; Turski and Schwarcz, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Less than 10% of KYNA is expected to remain during the probe test when infused 45 min prior.
source: Based on the timing of our experiments (the probe session was conducted 45 min after drug infusion,~3 half-lives), less than 10% of KYNA is expected to remain during the probe test.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the known half-life of KYNA.

claim: Injection of KYNA before satiation is expected to only disrupt activity during the period of satiation and not during the sated probe test.
source: Thus, injection before satiation is expected to only disrupt activity during the period of satiation and not during the sated probe test.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known duration of action of KYNA.

claim: Lower doses of KYNA infused immediately prior to the sated probe did not impact performance in two monkeys.
source: We confirmed, in two monkeys, that lower doses of KYNA infused immediately prior to the sated probe (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), did not impact performance.
evidence: This is a finding from a control experiment, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Trace amounts of KYNA remaining when infused prior to satiation are unlikely to be sufficient to impact behavior during the probe test.
source: Thus the trace amounts of KYNA remaining when infused prior to satiation are unlikely to be sufficient to impact behavior during the probe test.
evidence: This is an inference based on the control experiment with lower doses of KYNA.

claim: KYNA infusion either during satiation, or before the sated probe test, impaired the devaluation effect.
source: KYNA infusion either during satiation, or before the sated probe test, impaired the devaluation effect (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The impairment of devaluation by KYNA was evident in all three subjects.
source: This pattern was evident in all three subjects, resulting in a significant main effect (F1.0,2.1=52.3; p=0.017) with both test conditions differing significantly from saline-infused control sessions (Infusion before satiation: p=0.021, Infusion before sated probe: p=0.021).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.
